#9622. Is sharenting safe? 7 ways to mindfully post about your kids online

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your kid loses their first tooth or says something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button. For a lot of parents and caregivers, posting these moments feels like second nature.

Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting. And while it’s often a simple way to stay connected, it also puts your child’s story online before they can choose to share it. If you’ve started to wonder about the risks, it’s a good time to take stock of your posting habits.

Here's a look at why parents share and what’s worth knowing about the risks, plus seven small shifts to help you post with confidence.

Sharenting is when parents or caregivers post about their kids on social media. It could be a single birthday photo, or years of posts documenting a whole childhood. Think videos, funny quotes, school updates, potty-training wins, and even ultrasound pictures from before the baby arrives.

It's also widespread. Research reviews estimate that about three in four parents share photos, stories, or videos of their kids online, and most use their children's real names.

Parents have always shared news about their kids through holiday letters, birth announcements, and photos mailed to relatives. Social media just made the audience much bigger, the posts more public, and the record harder to remove.

Most sharenting comes from a good place. You're proud of your kid and you want the people in your life to know. Studies on parents who post about their kids point to the same reasons:

Staying close: Photos and videos let faraway family and friends watch your child grow.

Celebrating and remembering: Posts mark your child’s milestones and give you something to scroll back through later.

Finding community: Other parents and caregivers can offer advice and a “me too” at 2am, when parenting feels isolating.

Feeling seen: A kind comment on a rough day reminds you that you’re doing okay.

💙 Feeling alone as a parent? Here’s how to deal with loneliness.

Sharing your kids online isn’t necessarily harmful. Still, a few risks are worth knowing about:

A lasting digital footprint. Screenshots, reshares, and archives mean a photo can outlast the original post. Many kids have years of photos online before they're old enough to understand who can see them.

Personal information. Someone could piece together a full name, birth date, hometown, and school from a handful of posts. Over time, details like these may be misused for identity theft.

Location and background details. Location tags and details like a house number, school logo, or regular park in the background show where your child spends their time. On a public account, that can make their routine visible to strangers.

Facial recognition and AI. Photos on public accounts may be saved, scanned, or collected by AI tools and facial recognition software. Some of those tools turn ordinary photos into fake images.

💙 Want to bring more intention to parenting, online and off? Start here.

Before you hit share, take a breath and think about whether you want to post this moment. If you do, scan the photo and caption for anything that gives away too much, like a full name or a street sign.

For some structure, a short breathing exercise or meditation can help.

💙 Listen to Pause to Breathe with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

A couple of settings are worth checking before your next post. If your account is public, anyone can find and save your posts. Photos taken on your phone may also include the location where you took them.

Switch to a private account and remove followers you don’t know.

Turn off geotagging in your camera and app settings.

Platforms can change their defaults without warning, so it’s worth redoing this check every couple of months.

You can share the moment without giving away your child’s identity. Skip birth dates, school names, and daily routines. Use a nickname or first initial instead of your child’s full name.

Posting a day or two later makes it harder for anyone to know where your child is in real time.

Once your child is old enough to weigh in, show them the post and ask if they're okay with you sharing it. This shows them that their opinion matters. If your child is too young to decide, the next tip can help you decide for them.

Imagine your child at 25, seeing what you’re about to post. Does it give away something private about them, such as a health issue or a hard time at school? What seems relatable now may feel too personal to them later.

If you're unsure, keep the more personal moments in a private family group or an offline album.

💙 Explore Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your past posts felt right at the time, and it’s okay if some show more than you’d share today. Scroll back through your posts for details like full names, school names, or locations.

Delete the post, archive it, or move it to a private album if it feels too revealing.

You're not the only one with a camera. Grandparents, co-parents, babysitters, and friends may post photos of your child too, usually out of love and pride. A conversation up front about family boundaries keeps everyone on the same page.

leave full names and birth dates out of captions

skip location tags and recognizable landmarks in the background

use private groups or shared albums instead of public posts

💙 Calm’s Kind Communication session can help you find the words for a warm, open conversation.

Sharenting means posting about your child on social media, and the word blends "sharing" and "parenting." It covers anything from baby photos to regular updates as they grow up.

Common sharenting examples include ultrasound pictures, birthday posts, funny quotes, and health or milestone updates. Even a photo that seems harmless can reveal more than you intended, like a club sign or a team jersey in the background.

Many parents share to stay connected and celebrate their kids. Sharenting keeps faraway family members in the loop and connects you with other parents who get it. During hard stretches, it can help you feel less alone.

The main risks of sharenting include a lasting digital footprint and exposed personal details. Photos can be saved, reshared, or collected by AI tools, which is why child safety groups encourage private accounts.

That said, many posts don’t lead to harm, and small habits like turning off location tags help lower the risks further.

Sharenting shapes your child’s public image before they’re old enough to agree to it. Names, schools, and tagged locations can also reveal their routines to strangers, and a handful of details may be used for identity theft.

If you keep personal moments offline now, your child has more room to shape their own image as they grow.

There's no set age for when kids should have a say in what you post. Young kids may not fully understand what sharing means, so the decision starts with you. You can start asking as soon as they’re able to weigh in, and give their yes or no more weight as they grow.

#9621. A Parachute for Your ADHD Medication Crash

Most people taking ADHD medication experience an afternoon crash. Here, ADDitude readers reveal effective strategies for a softer landing.

It’s 4 p.m. and your brain is suddenly caught in a riptide. You feel like a swimmer fighting a strong current. The focus, priorities, and momentum that have propelled you forward until now are submerged under a layer of brain fog that rolls in around the same time each day.

This phenomenon is called the ADHD medication crash, and it happens to two-thirds of ADDitude readers who take ADHD medication. When medication levels drop rapidly in the bloodstream, this can result in fatigue, slowed processing speed, and inertia.

According to 3,500 ADDitude survey responses, 57 to 78 percent of stimulant medication users experience a regular crash, with dextroamphetamine and Ritalin LA users reporting the highest prevalence. Even people taking the most popular stimulant medications reported crash prevalence rates of near or above 60 percent. (Users’ experiences with the most popular stimulant medications are shown in the chart below.) The lowest crash prevalence rates were reported by people taking the non-stimulant medications Atomoxetine/Strattera (40%) and guanfacine (52.9%), suggesting that medication crashes are less common with non-stimulant ADHD treatments.

The most common signs of a medication crash, according to ADDitude readers who experience them, include:

The odds of a medication crash increase when an individual is experiencing stress, inadequate sleep, poor diet, and lack of exercise, according to survey respondents. Almost two-thirds of women who experience crashes said their menstrual cycle impacts the crash symptom severity. Readers did not cite medication interactions or caffeine as significant contributors.

The ability to manage household responsibilities is “often” or “always” impaired by medication crashes for 70 percent of survey respondents. Half of crashers say work responsibilities “often” or “always” suffer, and 43 percent say social and family interactions suffer.

#9620. 128 graduation wishes and messages for every graduate

Graduation is so much more than a diploma. It’s often the beginning of a big, uncertain shift into the unknowns of adulthood, a new career, and a life that’s far less defined than it was when you were a student. For some grads, this shift is an exciting one. For others, it’s terrifying. And many feel both.

If someone you love is graduating, you may want to write them a message that honors this journey. You want your note to feel personal, thoughtful, and maybe even a little inspiring — but finding the right words isn’t always easy.

The good news is you don’t need to be poetic or profound to share a meaningful sentiment on your loved one’s special day. A simple, warm message that acknowledges the moment and the person is more than enough. Whether you’re writing to a high school senior, a college grad, or someone finishing their doctorate, we’ve pulled together graduation wishes that are thoughtful, grounded, and easy to make your own.

The best wishes are the ones that make the graduate feel seen and loved. You recognize all the effort they’ve put in and offer encouragement without adding expectations.

Here are four aspects of a great graduation wish:

It’s genuine: A heartfelt “I’m proud of you” means more than a forced life lesson.

It reflects your relationship: Speak the way you typically would with them. If you’re usually lighthearted, stay lighthearted. If you’re more heartfelt and earnest, go that route.

It acknowledges the transition: Graduation is a moment of change, which can be both exciting and uncertain. Acknowledging this can help bring relief to the graduate.

It avoids pressure: Avoid mapping out their future or telling them what’s next, as this can add pressure. Instead, aim for something like, “Whatever comes next, I believe you’ll succeed.”

Graduation cards can have a tendency to lean on phrases like “Wishing you all the best!” and “The future is yours!” On the surface level, these messages can be sweet, but they don’t always reflect the depth of the relationship you’ve built.

If you want the graduate in your life to feel seen by you, here are 72 wishes that can help you out.

Watching your child graduate may leave you feeling pretty emotional. Here are eight ways to honor their accomplishment and the person they’ve become:

Seeing you graduate makes me beam. I’m so proud of you.

Your hard work and determination have paid off big time. Let’s celebrate!

I’m so proud of the person you’ve become (and have always been).

This achievement is just the beginning. Can’t wait to see all that you do!

Every day you make us proud, but today especially. Congratulations!

Your journey has been inspiring. I’m honored to be your parent.

You graduated! Let’s celebrate this huge milestone. You earned it and then some.

Your future is bright, and I can’t wait to see it unfold.

Siblings often see the late-night essay writing and the quiet doubts their siblings experience. To reflect that, here are eight wishes that are both playful and heartfelt:

I’ve seen every late-night study session and all the hair-pulling that got you here. You earned this.

No one works harder than you, and look at what it led to. Congrats!

Watching you grow into yourself has been the best part of being your sibling. (Now, could you stop growing? You’re making me look bad.)

So proud to call you my sibling and even prouder to celebrate this with you.

You’re my favorite hustler. And you did it all without losing who you are. Congratulations!

Thanks for graduating so Mom and Dad can focus on you for a bit, and I can act out without them noticing.

Congratulations to the second-smartest kid in the family. (Just kidding!) I love you and I’m so proud of you.

I hope you’re taking a second to soak it all in. You deserve it. (Okay, that’s enough gushing. As your sibling, it’s my job to keep your ego in check!)

Your friends have seen you at your best and worst and everything in between. Here are eight ways to reflect that journey with warmth and honesty:

You finally graduated! Now, can we finally book a trip to celebrate in style?

You can get a full night’s rest now. Congratulations!

Hope you’re ready for me to be very obnoxious and introduce you as “doctor” from now on.

Start stretching now, because this is huge, and we’re going to dance until morning to celebrate it properly!

I’m lucky to call you a friend. Congratulations. I’m beyond proud.

You’re the hardest worker I know. Congrats. You deserve it!

Get ready to be embarrassed: Nobody is going to have a louder cheering section at graduation than you. Love you!

You’re so impressive, and I learn so much from you all the time. Congratulations, friend!

If you’re a cousin, grandparent, aunt, or uncle, here are eight wishes that you can show support:

I’ve seen all the behind-the-scenes work that went into this moment. You’ve earned every bit of it.

You are so strong and resilient. I had no doubt this day would come. Congratulations!

You’ve grown into someone who leads with compassion and courage. It’s been a privilege to witness that.

This moment belongs to you. Now, let’s celebrate!

Congratulations on a job well done. “Proud” is an understatement.

Your dedication and heart are incredible to witness. Thanks for showing us how it’s done. Congrats!

I’m standing up a little taller today because you’re a part of our family. Congratulations.

Your tenacity and kindness are an inspiration. We love you and congrats!

What a joy to watch your grandchild graduate. Here are eight wishes that emphasize your love, pride, and admiration:

Watching you hit this milestone has made me so happy. Can’t wait to see all the other ones you reach.

You make this family proud every single day, but today especially. Congratulations!

This diploma is just the beginning. I love you and congratulations.

You’ve made your grandparents grin from ear to ear. Congratulations.

You did something incredible, and we’ve loved every moment of cheering you on.

I’m so happy I got to witness this day. You’re very special, and you make the world a better place.

Congratulations. But I’m not surprised at all. I’ve seen your work ethic, and I’ve seen your heart. This is just the start.

May this achievement remind you how deeply you’re loved, and of how deeply proud we are of you every single day.

Here are eight ways to say “I see you” to your partner and celebrate their big win:

Every day I stare at you in awe, but today even more so. Congratulations, I love you.

I saw firsthand how hard you worked for this. No one deserves this more than you.

You’ve earned every bit of this joy, and I’m so lucky to share it with you.

Hey, smartypants. Congrats! I love you, and I can’t believe I get to share my life with you.

You never needed a diploma to impress me. You’ve already done that just by being you (and with your killer back rubs).

The world is your oyster, and I’m so happy to be in the sea near you, watching you thrive.

You’ve built something incredible. I hope today you let yourself really feel that. Tonight, we’re celebrating!

This is just one of many moments I’m proud to be your partner. You’re the coolest, plain and simple.

Wish your work wife or colleague congratulations with these eight respectful and supportive messages:

Congratulations on your graduation! It’s inspiring to see. Great job!

If you’ve had the privilege of guiding a graduate, here are eight sincere wishes you can send them:

Your growth and success have been a joy to witness. (I had no doubt.)

Wishing you all the success! You deserve it. Congratulations.

Congratulations on this wonderful achievement. Here’s to you!

Messages from chosen family or supportive figures can be incredibly affirming. Here are eight wishes to celebrate the graduate in your life:

This journey has been nothing short of incredible. I’m so honored to witness it.

I hope you feel every ounce of pride and love coming your way today. Congratulations!

From all your loved ones, we see you. We’re so proud.

What a gift it’s been to watch you achieve your goal. Here’s to you!

You’ve earned every cheer and moment of this celebration. Congratulations!

Congrats! Your success is truly inspiring — and you did it with integrity, too.

Each type of graduation can bring its own set of emotions. It can bring excitement at a first leap into independence, anxiety at what’s next, or joy at crossing a finish line that took years to reach.

Grown-ups can include a message like this in cards, scrapbooks, or yearbooks for their little one:

Today is the start of your big, beautiful learning adventure. Yay!

Congratulations! You did it. May your next chapter be full of growth and laughter.

You passed with flying colors! We’re so proud of all of your growth.

This chapter had tons of challenges, and you tackled them all with grace. We love you!

You’ve proven you can do big things, and we’re unbelievably proud of you.

You’re amazing. Keep learning, keep asking questions, and keep being you.

You’re growing up with grace and self-confidence. We’re so happy to be along for the ride.

Congratulations! I’m sure you’re feeling a lot of emotions right now, but remember, you don’t need to have it all figured out. Just take it one step at a time.

Here are eight messages that reflect the respect and pride you have for adult learners balancing school with work, family, or caregiving:

Congrats! You accomplished something incredibly hard, and I'm so proud of you.

I’m unbelievably proud of you. You juggled so much to get here, and it didn’t go unnoticed.

Whether they’ve earned a PhD, MD, JD, or another credential, these grads have invested significant time, energy, and identity into their achievement. Here are eight ways to honor them and this huge milestone:

Congratulations! I’m bragging about you to everyone I know.

I have my fingers crossed that less time in the library means more time with me. So proud of you. Congratulations!

Good wishes for high school graduates should be grounded in encouragement. This is a time when everything feels new and a little uncertain. The best messages usually strike a balance between celebrating a significant achievement and acknowledging the emotional weight of leaving behind the familiar.

You might say something like: “You just accomplished something huge. Congratulations! And remember, it’s more than okay if the next step still feels a little uncertain.” This way, you’re honoring their hard work but also reminding them that they don’t need to have everything figured out yet.

Start by acknowledging the journey they’ve been on. College is typically full of academic pressure and personal growth. Let them know how proud you are of the person they’ve become.

You might say something like, “You’ve worked so hard, and I can’t wait to see what comes next. I’m so proud of the incredible person you are.”

Congratulate them, then add one kind thing about them. A few lines is plenty for a card. Here are some words for a graduation card, from short greetings to more personal notes:

"Congrats, grad! Your future is lucky to have you."

"Congratulations, graduate! I'm so proud of you."

"I've seen how much effort this took. I hope you feel so proud today."

"You kept going, even when things were hard. That says so much about who you are."

A good way to personalize a message is to reflect on what you admire about the graduate or how you’ve seen them evolve. Try naming something specific, like a moment they overcame something, or how they’ve impacted you.

Remember, you don’t need to write a long note. A short message like, “You’ve always led with compassion, and I admire that so much,” is powerful.

Funny graduation wishes are okay — just make sure the tone matches the moment. A light joke about student loans, caffeine dependency, or group projects gone wrong can land if it feels warm and comes from a place of love.

But as a rule of thumb, aim to avoid anything that pokes fun at their future or compares them to others.

A short message can still carry a lot of heart if it’s honest and specific. Here are a few examples that speak to a person’s strength and growth.

“You did it even when it felt impossible, and that says everything about how strong you are.”

“You poured your sweat and tears into this and earned every moment of it. I’m beyond proud.”

“I couldn’t be prouder of you and can’t wait to see what you do next.”

A good congratulations message for a graduate does two things. It says congratulations in plain words, and it names one thing you admire, like how hard they worked.

How you deliver it matters too. In person, a hug and “I’m so proud of you” mean a lot. In a card or text, you might write, “Congratulations on your graduation! I’ve loved watching you work toward this day.” Skip questions about what comes next. Many grads are still figuring that out, and today is for celebrating what they’ve done.

Start with congratulations, then add one thing you've loved watching her do. A line or two is plenty for a card. Here are short graduation messages for a granddaughter, whether she's finishing high school, college, or another program:

"So proud of you, my granddaughter. Congratulations on your graduation!"

"Watching you become who you are has been one of the great joys of my life. Congratulations, sweetheart."

"You're a very special young woman, and I'm so proud of all you've worked for. Congratulations!"

"You made it through high school, and I couldn't be prouder. Whatever comes next, you have my love."

"A college degree! Granddaughter, you've made me so proud. Congratulations."

"Being your grandma has been one of the best parts of my life. Congratulations, graduate!"

Congratulate the achievement and acknowledge the time it took. A doctorate often means years of research and writing, so mentioning that effort shows you see it. A line or two is enough. Here are a few short messages for a PhD or doctorate degree:

"Congratulations on completing your PhD. I've loved watching you work toward this day."

"You earned this doctorate through years of hard work. So proud of you!"

"Congratulations on your doctorate degree. I hope you take time to enjoy this one."

#9619. The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

Delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

Imagine two children entering first grade:

Jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

His parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment plan. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

[Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”]

Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

Year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

[Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?]

A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

The differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

The findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

This raises an important question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

Universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

Many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

Growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

For many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

#9618. Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

At Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

It’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins says these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”

Mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something new. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

It was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

As I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In our Dickinson College episode, that choice shows up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates.    Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

The choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

At Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones

In my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

When Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates new points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang

Working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It shows that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

Iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too important to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#9617. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

#9616. How to stop emotional flooding from disrupting your relationships

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The argument started with the dishes. Now you're saying something you know you’ll regret. Two minutes ago, you were mildly annoyed. Now your heart is pounding, and you can barely hear your partner over the noise in your own head.

This is emotional flooding, and it can happen to anyone. It isn’t a character flaw, and it doesn’t mean you're bad at relationships. When emotions run hot, the level-headed version of you can seem to vanish.

Flooding tends to show up when you're close to someone and the stakes feel personal. Fortunately, if you spot the signs early, you can keep an argument from turning into a blowup. Ahead, we’ll explore the science behind emotional flooding and how to calm yourself when it hits.

Emotional flooding is a state of overwhelm during a heated moment, usually a conflict. The term comes from John Gottman, PhD, who describes flooding as the point when you’re so overloaded that you can't take in new information, solve the problem, or hear the person in front of you.

Gottman and his colleague Robert Levenson studied couples at the University of Washington. As partners argued, they tracked physical signals like heart rate. Couples whose bodies showed higher arousal during conflict tended to grow less satisfied with their relationship over the following years.

Flooding feels different from person to person, so you may notice some of these signs but not others. Here's what to look for:

Racing heart: Your pulse climbs, and you feel your heartbeat in your chest or throat.

Fast, shallow breathing: Your breaths come quick and tight, and a full inhale feels out of reach.

Heat and tension: Your face flushes, and your jaw or shoulders tighten.

Tunnel vision: Your thinking narrows, and the other person’s words get hard to follow.

Urge to fight or flee: You want to raise your voice or leave, and it feels difficult to hold back.

Numbness or blankness: Your thoughts freeze, and you feel disconnected from the conversation.

Emotional flooding involves the amygdala, the part of your brain built to detect danger and keep you safe. When it senses a threat, it triggers the stress response and releases a surge of hormones that put your body on high alert. Adrenaline and norepinephrine speed up your heart rate and pull your focus toward the threat. That narrowed focus is part of why listening gets so hard.

In an everyday disagreement, there’s usually no physical danger, but your brain can still treat a raised voice or a difference of opinion as a threat, setting off the same alarm and the same rush of anger.

In close relationships, flooding may get extra fuel. Arguments can touch things that matter deeply to you, like feeling respected or safe. Old wounds and fear of where the fight might lead can pile on top of the present moment.

A note on relationships that don’t feel safe: This article is about everyday arguments, not abuse. If a raised voice or a pattern of control leaves you afraid of your partner, that fear isn’t a false alarm. Self-soothing isn’t the tool for this, and your safety comes first. You can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.

You can't always stop flooding before it starts, but you can help your body calm down once you realize it’s happening. Then, when you feel settled enough to think clearly again, you can gently return to the conversation. The tips below follow that order: calm your body first, then come back and repair. Try the ones that fit the moment, and skip any that don’t feel right for you.

The moment you notice your heart racing or your thoughts scrambling, tell yourself “this is flooding.” Naming it reminds you that the feeling is physical and temporary. That bit of awareness gives you room to choose your next move instead of reacting on autopilot.

💙 Try the Full Sensory Awareness meditation on the Calm app.

A longer exhale engages your parasympathetic nervous system, the part of your nervous system that helps you rest and settle down.

In one study, people who practiced cyclic sighing (also known as the physiological sigh), a breathing pattern of two quick inhales and one long exhale, reported bigger mood improvements than those who practiced mindfulness meditation.

If breathing exercises feel uncomfortable, skip ahead to the next tip.

💙 Press play on the Breathe to Calm Down session on Calm.

When you're flooded, stepping away can help you collect yourself before you talk things through. Tell your partner you need a break and that you’ll come back, so they don’t feel abandoned mid-conflict.

According to Gottman's research, it can take at least 20 minutes for your body to calm back down, so give yourself enough time. If you can’t leave the room, even a few minutes of silence can help.

Your body often responds to physical cues faster than logic. Use your time-out to splash cold water on your face or step outside for a few minutes of fresh air. Either one can help slow your heart rate.

💙 If anger is running hot, listen to Calm’s Investigating Anger session.

Flooding releases stress hormones that prepare your body for action. A brisk walk, or any gentle movement that suits you, gives that energy somewhere to go instead of letting it build.

💙 Explore Dr. Eric López's Walk Away Stress series on Calm.

Once it feels calmer, return to your partner. You don't have to solve everything right away. A short repair can open the door to trying again.

Try: “I got overwhelmed earlier. Can we try again?”

Gottman’s work suggests that how couples repair after conflict is a key predictor of long-term satisfaction, often more telling than how often they fight.

💙 Learn how couples meditation can strengthen your relationship.

Emotional flooding is feeling so overwhelmed during a conflict or another intense moment that you can’t think clearly or listen. The term comes from psychologist John Gottman's research on couples.

A common example of emotional flooding is a tense meeting with your boss, when your heart starts pounding and your mind goes blank. It can also happen at home, like when a conversation with a family member or partner escalates.

💙 Check out how to deal with a conflict at work.

Emotional flooding is a surge of intense emotion in a specific moment, while emotional dysregulation is ongoing difficulty managing emotions across a range of situations. Flooding can be one sign of dysregulation, but if it happens now and then, that doesn’t necessarily mean you have a pattern of dysregulation.

Emotional flooding can be more common and more intense for people with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). Studies show that trouble managing emotions is a core part of ADHD in adults. With ADHD, you may flood more often or take longer to calm down.

If flooding feels constant or unmanageable, a doctor can help you figure out what’s behind it.

💙 Learn what ADHD shutdown is and how to manage it.

You can stop being emotionally flooded by giving your body time to settle before you continue the conversation. Take a break of at least 20 minutes, and try long exhales, cold water on your face, or a brisk walk. When you feel more grounded, give the conversation another try.

Mindfulness can help with emotional flooding because it trains you to notice early signs, such as a racing heart or a tight jaw, before they build. Over time, that gives you a chance to pause instead of react in hard moments.

Try to practice mindfulness when you’re calm, with short breathing exercises or guided meditation, so the skill is there when you need it.

#9615. Paul Hamlyn Foundation announces recipients of £75,000 Awards for Artists

Award winners left to right: Hayley Tompkins, Daudi Matsiko, Bushra El-Turk, Linda Bell, Olivia Chaney, Rory Pilgrim, Ayanna Witter-Johnson, Georgina Starr, Charlotte Keeffe, (Racheal Crowther not present).Photo credit: Emile Holba

The Turner prize nominee Rory Pilgrim and the Venice Biennale artist Hayley Tompkins are among the recipients of this year’s Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s Awards for Artists. The £75,000 awards were granted to five artists and five composers.

In the wake of the ongoing cost of living crisis, the awards are timely. “Unique in its no-strings-attached funding model, the [Hamlyn] awards for artists allows recipients to use their award as they wish, providing them the freedom to develop their creative ideas, alleviating the pressures they may be facing,” says a press statement.

Tompkins was part of a trio of artists, alongside Corin Sworn and Duncan Campbell, who showed works in the Scotland + Venice exhibition in 2013. Her installations combine painting with a variety of other media, including found objects, digital films, photography and furniture. “It still hasn’t felt real yet, but I do know with more resources there will be room for me to feel and move a bit differently now,” she says in a statement.

Pilgrim’s work explores how “activism, spirituality and music can create spaces for connection”, adds the statement. Bristol-born Pilgrim was nominated for the Turner Prize in 2023 for their commission RAFTS at Serpentine Galleries and Barking Town Hall. “After working on many intensive processes, [the award] gives invaluable breathing space, autonomy and financial security to find joy and excitement in creativity,” Pilgrim says.

The other successful artists this year are Georgina Starr, who is known for performance works such as Androgynous Egg (2017), Dublin-born artist Racheal Crowther and the learning disabled artist Linda Bell. Judges include Joe Hill, the director of Yorkshire Sculpture Park, Melissa Blanchflower, a senior curator at Turner Contemporary in Margate, and Sheryll Catto, the artistic director of ActionSpace.

Since 1994, Paul Hamlyn Foundation has made 377 awards to artists with over £12m in funding; Phyllida Barlow, Yinka Shonibare and Alberta Whittle are among the previous recipients. Five composers including Daudi Matsiko and Ayanna Witter-Johnson were also recognised.

Winning a prize can give an artist international exposure, but the question of who really benefits—critically and commercially—is an increasingly vexed one

#9612. 101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?

Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question. It’s almost like they’re professionally trained in the art of dodging conversation.

The thing is, kids actually do want to talk. You just have to ask the right questions: ones that spark their imagination, make them laugh, or invite them to share something meaningful on their terms.

So, meet them where they are. Instead of the same old, “How was your day?” (which, let’s be honest, will never yield a thrilling response), try questions that make them pause and think for a moment. This way, you’re not prying information out of them, you’re building a habit of open conversation, one fun question at a time.

Ask them in the car, at bedtime, over breakfast, or whenever your kid is in a chatty mood. You might be surprised at what they share — and the hilarious, heartwarming, or even unexpectedly deep conversations that follow.

Laughter is one of the easiest ways to connect with your child (and can boost your mental health too). These offbeat, ridiculous questions will get them giggling while giving you a glimpse into their wonderfully weird little minds.

Would you rather have a banana for a nose or popcorn for ears? Kids love absurd choices, and these “would you rather” questions are a surefire way to spark hilarious debates.

Would you rather have spaghetti for hair or marshmallows for fingers?

Would you rather live in a house made of chocolate or a castle made of cheese?

Would you rather always talk in rhymes or only be able to whisper?

Would you rather ride a roller coaster that never ends or a Ferris wheel that goes super fast?

Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?

Ever wonder what your backpack thinks about your daily routine? These questions help kids think outside the box — and maybe appreciate their favorite objects a little more.

If your socks could talk, what would they say about your feet?

If your toothbrush had feelings, how would it feel about its job?

If your toys threw a party while you were sleeping, what would they do?

If your backpack could complain, what would it say?

If animals could talk to you, which one do you think would be the funniest?

What if the moon really was made of cheese? These questions let kids build wild, imaginary worlds where anything is possible.

If you could invent a new holiday, what would it be called and how would we celebrate?

If your shadow had a mind of its own, what do you think it would do?

If you could make one silly law that everyone had to follow, what would it be?

If you had a magic remote that could pause or rewind real life, when would you use it?

What’s better than food? Food-related nonsense! These questions are perfect for mealtime giggles.

What’s the silliest pizza topping combination you can think of?

If you could turn any food into a superhero, which one would you pick and why?

If vegetables could talk, which one would be the grumpiest?

If you ate only dessert for an entire day, which treats would you choose?

If you could invent a new ice cream flavor, what would it be?

💙 Why not incorporate some silly moves into your kids day with Mel Mah’s Working Out the Wiggles session?

Forget the usual “What’s your favorite color?” These questions dig a little deeper into what makes your child them — their dreams, their interests, and how they see the world.

Who are they, really? These questions help kids define what makes them special. Who knows? They might even surprise themselves with their answers.

What’s something you love doing that makes you feel really happy?

If you could rename yourself, what would you want to be called?

What’s one thing that makes you feel really proud of yourself?

If you had to describe yourself in three words, what would they be?

Every kid has dreams. These questions encourage them to think big.

If you could have any job in the world when you grow up, what would it be?

If you could live anywhere in the world, where would it be?

If you could suddenly have super-skill, what would it be?

If you could invent something to make life easier, what would it do?

What’s something you dream about doing one day?

What’s school really like? What do they wish adults understood? These questions help you see the world through their eyes.

If you could be principal of your school for a day, what rules would you change?

What’s one thing about school that you really like?

What’s one thing about school you wish was different?

What’s one thing you wish adults understood about being a kid?

Forget the usual “favorite color” and “favorite food” questions — these favorites are a little more unexpected.

If you could only listen to one song forever, what would it be?

If you could only watch one movie over and over again, which one would you pick?

If you could only eat three foods for a year, what would they be?

What book should everyone read at least once?

If you were a baseball player, what song would play when you came up to bat?

These questions help kids think outside the box and explore new ideas — without it feeling like homework.

What if everything was upside down? What if people lived in the ocean? These questions let kids stretch their creativity and invent a world of their own.

If you could switch lives with any fictional character, who would it be?

If you could time travel, would you rather visit the past or the future?

If you could build a brand-new planet, what would it be like?

If you could talk to any historical figure, who would you pick and what would you ask?

If you could live in any book or movie world, which one would you choose?

Kids love hypotheticals, especially ridiculous ones. These questions tap into their curiosity and creativity.

If aliens landed in our backyard, what would be the first thing you’d say to them?

If you could talk to animals, what’s the first thing you’d ask them?

If you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

If you could be invisible for a day, what would you do?

If you could wake up with a superpower, which one would you want?

Kids are natural philosophers. Sometimes, they just need the right question to get them going.

What’s something you’ve always been curious about but never asked?

If you could solve one big mystery in the world, what would it be?

If you could design your dream school, what classes would you add?

What’s something that happens in nature that seems magical to you?

What do you think is the coolest invention ever made?

These questions encourage kids to see things in a new way, whether it’s about themselves, the world, or the future.

What’s something small that can make a big difference?

What’s a time when you changed your mind about something?

If you could ask the president one question, what would it be?

What’s one way kids can change the world?

What’s something you wish you knew how to do?

Kids may not always have the words to explain their feelings, but these thoughtful questions help create a safe space for them to share what’s in their hearts. The Feelings Wheel can be a good visual aid for this too.

Sometimes, kids just need the right words to talk about how they feel. These questions give them a way to open up.

What’s something that made you feel really happy this week?

What’s a time when you felt really proud of yourself?

What’s something that always makes you feel loved?

What’s a time when you felt really brave?

What’s something you wish people knew about you?

It’s not always easy to talk about the hard stuff, but these questions can help kids express their feelings in a safe way.

What’s something that helps you feel better when you’re sad?

What’s a time when something felt really hard, but you got through it?

What’s one thing that makes you feel nervous?

What’s something you do when you’re feeling frustrated?

What’s a time when someone helped you feel better?

Friends are a huge part of kids’ lives — these questions help them reflect on what friendship means to them.

What do you think makes someone a good friend?

What’s one way you like to show kindness to others?

What do your friends do to make you feel special?

What’s something you love doing with your family?

If you could plan the perfect day with your best friend, what would you do?

Slowing down and noticing the good things is a skill kids can carry with them for life. These questions make space for reflection.

What’s something you’re really grateful for today?

What’s a small thing that makes a big difference in your day?

What’s a memory that always makes you smile?

What’s something you love about yourself?

What’s one thing you want to remember about being a kid when you’re older?

These questions are designed to spark deeper connections and create shared experiences — because the best conversations are about connecting.

Every family has inside jokes, traditions, and funny moments. These questions bring them to the surface.

If you could plan a dream family vacation, where would we go?

What’s something funny that has happened in our family?

What’s a meal we should cook together soon?

If we could create a secret family handshake, what would it look like?

Remember that time we all got soaked in the rain? Or the time you laughed so hard you snorted? These questions help relive the best moments.

What’s something we’ve done together that made you laugh really hard?

What’s the silliest story I’ve ever told you?

What’s one thing we should do more often as a family?

What’s next for our family? These questions invite kids to dream up exciting adventures — real or imagined.

If we could go on a wild adventure tomorrow, what would we do?

What’s a hobby or activity you’d love for us to try together?

If you could design the perfect family game night, what would we play?

If we could time travel together, what era would we visit?

If we started a family business, what would we sell?

Every family has its own kind of magic. These questions bring it out in unexpected ways.

If our family had a theme song, what would it be?

If we could invent a new family tradition, what would it be?

If you could give everyone in our family a superpower, what would they be?

If every member of our family was an animal, what would it be?

What’s a way we can make someone else’s day better together?

What’s one thing you want me to always remember about you?

💙 Mel Mah’s Kids Bedtime Routine can help you all wind down in a peaceful way, together.

The best questions to ask kids are open-ended, playful, and relevant to their world. Instead of asking, “Did you have a good day?”—which almost always leads to a dead-end answer—try something that sparks their imagination or invites storytelling, like “What was the funniest thing that happened today?” or “If you could switch places with your teacher for a day, what would you do?” Kids are much more likely to engage when a question feels fun, unexpected, and free of pressure.

Kids love absurdity, so the weirder and wackier the question, the better. Offbeat questions tap into their creativity, making conversation feel more like a game than a chore.

Silly questions are also a great way to bond, especially when you play along. If your kid tells you they’d rather ride a roller coaster that never stops over a Ferris wheel that goes super fast, ask why and join in the fun by sharing your own ridiculous answer.

Laughter is a powerful connector, and sometimes the most unexpected conversations start with a totally goofy question.

For 6-year-olds, short questions about things they can picture work best. Silly choices and pretend play go over well. Try “What would you name a pet cloud?” or “If your stuffed animals had jobs, what would they be?” Many of the funny questions above fit this age, especially the “would you rather” and “If your stuff could talk” lists. Ask one question at a time, since young kids can lose the thread when you ask two at once.

Which question to ask depends on what you want from the chat. If you want laughs, pick a “would you rather” or other funny question. If you want to know your child better, choose from the get-to-know list. For big feelings, try the emotional expression questions. When you’re not sure, start silly to help them relax, then move to a deeper one.

Kids spend a lot of their day being told what to do—sit still, follow directions, finish their homework—so having a space where they get to lead the conversation is powerful. Asking fun and engaging questions gives them a chance to express themselves, think creatively, and feel heard without any right or wrong answers. It also helps build communication skills, emotional intelligence, and a sense of connection with you.

Beyond that, these questions create opportunities for everyday bonding. A quick chat in the car or during dinner can turn into a meaningful moment of connection. The more kids feel like their thoughts and ideas are valued, the more likely they are to open up — not just about the silly stuff but about the big things, too.

The key to getting good answers is making the conversation feel natural, not forced. If you ask a question and get a one-word response, don’t panic — sometimes kids just need a little extra space to warm up. Try following up with, “Tell me more!” or sharing your own answer first to get the ball rolling. If they see that you’re genuinely interested (and willing to be a little silly yourself), they’ll be more likely to engage.

Also, be thoughtful about your timing. Some kids open up more when they’re relaxed—like at bedtime or when you’re doing an activity together—while others chat more when they’re distracted, like in the car. If they’re tired, hungry, or mid-screen time, you might not get much out of them. But if you catch them in the right moment, you might just unlock a goldmine of thoughts, ideas, and hilarious kid logic.

The best time to ask kids questions is when they’re naturally more open to conversation — when they feel safe, relaxed, and not pressured to respond. For some kids, that’s during bedtime, when they’re winding down and their thoughts start to flow. For others, it’s in the car, when there’s no pressure for eye contact and they can talk freely. Meal times, walks, or even while playing with Legos can also be great moments to slip in a fun question.

Trying to force deep conversation right after school when their brain is fried or when they’re engrossed in a game or show usually won’t work. Instead, look for organic, low-pressure moments when chatting feels easy. And remember, it’s not about when you ask, it’s about showing up consistently so that when they are ready to talk, they know you’ll be there to listen.
