#9611. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”

These people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another said, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”

Rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person said, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”

It’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person said.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly important for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”

Naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

That is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

According to an analysis of 99 studies, mental well-being leads to a longer life.

Generous parental leave policies improve health for moms and babies, family finances, and equality at work and at home.

#9610. Empathy vs compassion: the difference (with real-life examples)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Understanding and connecting with another person—either through empathy or compassion—facilitates more meaningful interactions and relationships. Whether it’s a friend going through a tough time or a family member facing a challenge, how we connect with them can significantly impact the support we offer.

Knowing the differences between empathy and compassion can help us approach others and what they’re going through with understanding and kindness.

Compassion is concern for another person's well-being and happiness, and a genuine urge to help alleviate their suffering. Compassion isn’t just a fleeting emotion — it’s a lasting state, a readiness to extend a helping hand whenever possible. (For the full definition, here’s our guide to what compassion is.)

Empathy is the capability to tune into someone else’s emotions and to feel what they’re feeling. Empathy means genuinely trying to understand another person’s feelings and perspective.

💙 Sharpen your listening skills and make others truly feel heard with Jay Shetty in this Supportive Listening meditation.

While both empathy and compassion are avenues to connect with others, their core essence and impact are different. While empathy allows for emotional understanding, compassion takes it further by driving action. It's about moving from feeling to doing, from emotional resonance to proactive kindness.

Through this understanding, we can see the value of cultivating empathy and practicing compassion in our daily actions, which not only enrich our relationships but positively impact our communities, too.

Empathy steers emotional connection. It's about feeling the same emotions that another person is experiencing and aligning emotionally because of that similarity. On the other hand, compassion drives us towards a deep understanding of another's distress, coupled with a desire to make them feel better. It's not just about feeling, it’s about understanding and taking action.

Empathy is rooted in deeply feeling what another person is going through and mirroring their emotional state. Compassion is about acknowledging what the other people are going through instead of feeling the emotion yourself.

Empathy often revolves around an inward reflection that allows us to feel the emotions that another person is experiencing. Compassion propels us outward and encourages acting on the feeling to help alleviate someone else’s discomfort.

Empathy primarily consists of feeling the emotional state of another, while compassion is action-oriented. Compassion prompts us to take steps to ease another's suffering, no matter how small.

Empathy, although a profound feeling, can be more of a momentary emotional connection that is often fleeting once the shared emotion dissipates. Compassion, on the other hand, reflects a long-term commitment to assisting others and a consistent readiness to help.

💙 Learn more about Empathy vs. Compassion with this Daily Jay session.

You usually won’t choose between them in the moment. They tend to show up together. Here’s how each one can look in the same situation.

Empathy is feeling with someone. Compassion is taking a step to help. You won’t usually pick one in the moment, since feeling with someone is often what leads you to help.

Empathy and compassion are ways to connect with others, but they play different roles. Empathy is about feeling the same emotions that someone else is feeling. For example, if a friend is sad, you feel sad along with them. Compassion takes empathy a step further. It’s about recognizing someone’s distress and wanting to help alleviate it. So, when you see someone in trouble, not only do you understand their problem, but you also want to help sort it out. Compassion motivates us to act and make a positive difference, while empathy encourages us to feel and relate.

Both empathy and compassion are valuable in building meaningful relationships. Empathy helps in understanding other people’s emotions and creating bonds. Compassion, however, not only understands but also propels us to take action to help. It’s about moving from feeling to doing something helpful. Empathy can be a stepping stone to compassion, leading us from feeling to taking positive action.

Being empathetic and compassionate is like having a superpower for creating solid and supportive relationships. Empathy allows you to understand others' feelings, while compassion motivates you to take action to help. It’s a blend that encourages understanding while making a positive impact in others’ lives. Empathy and compassion go hand in hand, enhancing our connections with others and making our social interactions more meaningful and enriching.

Empathetic and compassionate leadership both aim to create a supportive work environment, but they do so in slightly different ways. Empathetic leadership is about understanding employees' emotions and perspectives and creating an environment where people feel heard and understood. Compassionate leadership, on the other hand, not only understands but takes action to support and help employees, recognizing the challenges and actively working to provide support or solutions. Compassionate leadership often brings a more supportive and caring work culture, benefiting both employees and the organization.

#9609. World Kindness Day 2026: what it is and 7 ways to join in

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The barista is ringing up the person in front of you when their card gets declined. You lean over, tap your phone, and cover the $4. They turn around, flustered, and thank you twice. The line keeps moving, but your morning feels a bit lighter.

Moments like this are what World Kindness Day is all about. Every year on November 13, it celebrates how acts of goodwill can brighten an ordinary day, for those receiving and performing them.

Read on for the story behind the day, what the research says about kindness and mental health, and some simple ways to take part, whatever your schedule looks like.

World Kindness Day is an unofficial global observance that encourages acts of kindness, big and small. In 2026, it falls on Friday, November 13. The day was first observed in 1998 and grew out of the World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations rather than a single founder.

The coalition formed at a conference in Tokyo, and it included founding members from Japan, Singapore, Australia, Canada, Thailand, the U.K., and the U.S. They chose November 13 because it was the conference’s opening day and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement. Today, classrooms, offices, and communities around the world honor the day.

You’ve probably felt it: you do something kind and your mood instantly lifts. Researchers have studied this effect, and here’s what they’ve found.

In a 2023 study from The Ohio State University, 122 adults with moderate to severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assigned to one of three activities for several weeks. They either did acts of kindness, planned social activities, or practiced cognitive reappraisal, which means looking at a stressful event from a new angle.

All three activities helped, but kindness did more than cognitive reappraisal to ease depression and anxiety. The kindness group was also the only one that reported feeling more connected to others.

Other research points the same way. A review of 27 studies covering more than 4,000 people showed that performing acts of kindness gave people a modest but noticeable boost in their well-being.

Kindness may also lighten a hard day. In a two-week diary study of 77 adults, people tracked their stress, their mood, and how they helped others each day. Stress usually dragged positive emotion down, but on high-stress days when people helped more than usual, their mood held steady. In other words, a little extra kindness seemed to cushion the blow of a stressful day.

A note on the research: Most of this research is short-term and relies on self-reported mood, so we can’t say how long the benefits last. Kindness can support your well-being, but it doesn’t replace professional care. If anxiety, low mood, or stress lasts for weeks, it’s worth talking to a doctor.

You don’t need a grand gesture. These seven ideas fit into a regular day, whether you’re at home, at work, or anywhere in between. You can also adjust any of them to fit your time, energy, and budget.

There’s probably someone on your mind — a friend you know is having a hard time, a relative you haven’t caught up with lately, or an old coworker you miss.

Mention the moment you thought of them, like “Saw a dog that looked like yours and had to say hi. Hope you’re doing okay.” Add “no need to reply” at the end, in case they’re feeling down or overwhelmed and might not have the energy for a back-and-forth.

💙 Before you send your message, read our guide to loving-kindness meditation.

Leave a short review for a small business, or send a note to a service worker who made your day. Write what you appreciated, such as the waiter who kept checking on your table or the mechanic who explained the repair without talking down to you.

For a coworker, send a note to their manager, who may not otherwise hear about their good work.

💙 Reflect on who you want to thank with the 7 Days of Gratitude course on Calm.

A quick “love your shoes” is nice, but a more specific compliment shows someone that you’re really paying attention, and that you care. Praise someone for how patient they were with a difficult customer or how useful their point was in the meeting.

It takes only a few seconds, but noticing the details can mean more to someone than you might expect.

💙 Sharpen your compliments with Jay Shetty’s Effective Praise session on Calm.

Look for small things that would make someone’s day better and take care of one: carry the heavy bag, refill the empty printer, or take on the household chore nobody wants to do.

When you spot a need early, you can spare someone the awkwardness of asking.

💙 Keep the kindness moving with Jay Shetty’s Pay It Forward session on Calm.

Buy lunch for your colleague, round up a tip, or add a friend’s drink to your order. Set an amount before you head out, so a kind impulse doesn’t turn into a money worry later.

If your budget is a concern, the next idea includes free ways to help.

Donate clothes you don’t wear to a shelter, give to a cause you care about, or sign up for a volunteer shift. When you donate, check what the organization needs first, since staff and volunteers have to sort through anything they can’t use.

Many organizations also offer remote tasks, like writing cards or tutoring online.

💙 Start close to home with Jay Shetty’s Community Service session on Calm.

Kindness toward yourself counts, and it’s often overlooked. Notice how you talk to yourself when something goes wrong, then ask whether you’d say it that way to a friend. If you wouldn’t, here’s a quick way to try a kinder tone.

Try: A short self-compassion pause. Place a hand on your chest, take one slow breath, and name how you feel (“this is a lot right now”). Then say what you’d tell a friend in the same situation (“that sounds hard”).

💙 Press play on Calm’s Friend on the Inside meditation with Jeff Warren.

The World Kindness Movement created the day to encourage kind acts around the world. For many people, it’s also an invitation to do the kind thing they’ve been putting off, like thanking a neighbor.

World Kindness Day in 2026 is on Friday, November 13. It falls on November 13 every year, so only the day of the week changes.

World Kindness Day is on November 13 because it was the opening day of the first World Kindness Movement conference in Tokyo, and the 35th anniversary of Japan’s Small Kindness Movement.

No single person started World Kindness Day. The World Kindness Movement, a coalition of kindness organizations from seven countries, launched the day in Tokyo.

No, World Kindness Day and Random Acts of Kindness Day are two separate observances. World Kindness Day is November 13, while Random Acts of Kindness Day is February 17. They share the same spirit, so you’re welcome to celebrate both.

Studies suggest kindness can be good for you. Acts of kindness have been linked to better mood, lower anxiety, and stronger connection with others.

In one diary study, stressful days usually made people feel less happy and upbeat. But on days when people helped others more than usual, that drop in positive feelings was smaller.

Kindness supports well-being, but it doesn’t replace care. Speak to a doctor if anxiety, stress, or low mood lasts for weeks.

💙 Here’s how you can lower your stress naturally.

If you’re feeling drained, it’s okay to start with yourself. A kind word to yourself counts, and some days it’s all you have energy for. When you have more to give, something small and thoughtful is plenty, like holding the door for someone or letting someone go ahead of you in line.

There’s no official color for World Kindness Day, so you can wear whatever feels good. Some schools and groups pick a color for their own events.

#9608. ICA Miami selects architect to renovate recently acquired building

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

The Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami) has appointed the global architecture firm Gensler to renovate a 30,000-sq.-ft building the museum acquired in 2024, doubling its exhibition and public-programming space.

Steps away from its current venue in Miami’s Design District, the new wing is scheduled to open in late 2027—as the museum marks its tenth anniversary at its current location. Focused on expanding the free museum’s community outreach, the project will transform the ICA into a multi-site complex and house the first permanent display of its collection.

The museum’s new building formerly housed the De la Cruz Collection, a private museum that closed after the 2024 death of its co-founder Rosa de la Cruz. Since its $25m acquisition later that year, the site has mainly hosted the ICA’s educational programmes. It will close once construction begins. The renovation is part of a $40m capital campaign, supported entirely by private funds.

The new design will adapt the existing structure. “The building was developed to house a contemporary art collection,” Alex Gartenfeld, the ICA’s director and chief curator, tells The Art Newspaper. “But with the spaces we are constructing, we intend to enhance the museum’s story-driven narrative approach to the collection and exhibitions.”

Rendering of ICA Miami’s new building Courtesy Gensler

Eight new galleries will occupy the building’s first and second floors. Among them will be the museum’s first dedicated spaces for its growing permanent collection of more than 2,000 works.

“The programme between the two buildings is blended, but we will now have two full floors dedicated to our permanent collection,” Gartenfeld says. “Around every six months, we will refresh the collection display to reflect the collection’s emphasis and recent acquisitions.”

The entire third floor will be dedicated to public programming, including talks, symposia, lectures and performances. “Beyond adding galleries, this renovation will strengthen the ICA’s ability to support artists, expand learning and create a platform for exchange and belonging in one of the world’s most dynamic cultural cities,” says Bevin Savage Yamazaki, Gensler’s global culture and museums leader.

A reimagined façade with transparent components is key to the design. Gartenfeld says the façade aims to provide a connection between street-level traffic and the museum itself.

The renovations focus on visitor experience and accessibility as well. The lobby will be redesigned. And reconfigured outdoor areas will include social spaces, a sculpture deck and an expanded café. “We are aiming to create a more collective experience,” Gartenfeld says.

The museum expanded its exhibition space and reorganised its permanent collection for the first time in almost 100 years—with a special focus on Native American art

#9607. AI anxiety: 5 ways to cope when you’re scared of AI

If you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone. Chief Clinical Officer at Calm, Chris Mosunic, PhD, has tips and strategies to help tame a growing source of anxiety.

AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing. It isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but the feelings are real and common. They can focus on everyday risks, such as job loss and AI-powered scams, and bigger ones, such as AI getting out of human control.

AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools. A 2023 Calm survey* found that nearly 1 in 3 U.S. adults (29%) felt anxious about AI, and 18% described their feelings as fear or dread. At the same time, 31% felt optimistic, and 31% felt excited. Many respondents felt a mix: amazed by AI and nervous about it.

Concern about AI has stayed high in the years since. In a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey, 52% of U.S. adults said they feel more concerned than excited about AI in daily life. That’s up from 37% in 2021 and about the same as in 2023. Just 9% said they feel more excited than concerned.

It’s hard to know how AI will affect our safety and our lives. You might wonder how it will change your job, what it could mean for areas like scientific research, and what the future will look like. Many of us find uncertainty hard to cope with, so feeling anxious or out of control is understandable. But when anxiety feels overwhelming, it can start to affect your sleep, mood, and focus.

These five ways to manage AI anxiety draw on mindfulness and common thinking traps, like catastrophizing. Start with whichever fits how you feel today.

The rapid rise in AI and automation can feel like a threat to our livelihoods (and even our lives), making many of us feel unstable and out of control.

Resist resisting: When confronted with uncertainty, our first instinct can often be to fight it. Try sitting with it instead. Notice how the discomfort shows up in your body and mind.

Go at your own pace: Give yourself time to adjust to the new realities of AI.

Talk it out: Process your anxieties with a friend or a coworker. You may find someone who feels the same way.

💙 On those days when you feel overwhelmed by the rapidly changing tech landscape, try a simple meditation practice like Pause to Breathe to help you feel more grounded.

If you’re feeling anxious or uneasy about AI, don’t invalidate or try to avoid those emotions — that approach can make things worse. Instead, let yourself feel anxious. Telling yourself you’re overreacting can damage your self-trust and self-confidence.

Identify the emotions: Get a better understanding of what you’re feeling. Your anxiety could mean you’re working through a more deeply rooted problem, like feeling threatened or inadequate.

Try meditation: Meditation can help you ground yourself in the present moment and tune into what you’re feeling and where it’s coming from.

Write down all your anxieties without censoring yourself: Set aside dedicated time each day to think through your anxious thoughts, helping you process and make sense of your emotions.

💙 Take some time to stop and do this short Emotions Check-In to make space for any anxious feelings.

When we’re feeling anxious about the unknown, many of us fall into the trap of catastrophic thinking, imagining the worst possible outcome, even without evidence to support it. This can cause low-level anxieties to spiral out of control.

Challenge your worst fears: What evidence do you have that they’re true or that they’ll happen?

Bring to mind times in the past that felt groundbreaking in the tech world: Think back to the creation of mobile phones, laptops, or even navigation apps, and consider how you’ve adapted to their existence despite any initial anxieties or concerns. The same could happen with AI.

Bring your mind back to the now: The future feels a whole lot less intimidating when you focus on the present.

💙 One of the best ways you can bring yourself back to the present is through mindfulness meditation, which you can learn in the Mindfulness for Beginners series.

Many of us find ourselves viewing situations as an all-or-nothing approach. This is a cognitive distortion called polarized thinking, and it often occurs because we’re focused on the extremes without considering the nuances or possibilities of any given situation.

The debate around AI is nuanced. Popular culture shows dystopian futures, so it can be easy to think there’s only one possible outcome with AI.

However, reality tends to exist in between the extremes, so remind yourself that it’s perfectly normal for opposing emotions or views to be present at the same time. And they can also all feel as strong, real, or true as each other. You can feel fascinated and terrified, anxious and excited, or resentful and grateful.

When we allow multiple truths to co-exist in our minds, we make space for more ease. So try to hold space for the contradictions and the possibilities.

💙 For a more in-depth discussion on how to use mindfulness to combat worrying and keep nuance at the forefront, check out the Overcome Stress & Anxiety series.

At the extreme end of AI anxiety, some of us may have a deep—even subconscious—fear about a machine taking over. We ask questions like: Is this the beginning of the end of humanity? Will humans be replaced by robots?

A fear of overdependence on technology can cause us to worry about the negative consequences of relying too heavily on artificial intelligence. One way to remedy this fear is to embrace our humanity.

Be present for the little things you often take for granted, like hugs, laughing until it hurts, or exchanging a look with your best friend.

Make time for the people in your life, and prioritize connecting with them face-to-face when you can.

Marvel at the awesomeness of human things like awkward silences or goosebumps when you’re listening to music.

Ask people how they’re really feeling and practice deep listening when they respond.

Disconnect from technology and spend time in nature.

💙 Embrace the power of being human and living in the now by reading a book, listening to a meditation, or taking a Mindful Walk.

*Calm research was fielded among n = 450 adults in the US between March 21, 2023 and March 22, 2023 and is nationally representative, with quotas across age, gender, race, ethnicity, and region.

Recent news stories have shown how general-purpose AI tools may respond in unsafe or harmful ways, especially when people are vulnerable or struggling with a mental health crisis. These situations are rare, but they highlight an important truth: AI is not human and can’t accurately recognize risk, provide crisis support, or understand the complexity of your emotional world.

AI can support mental health — especially when it’s part of a program designed and guided by licensed professionals. But general AI tools, like chatbots or large language models, are not a replacement for real human care.

If you’re struggling, please consider reaching out to a therapist or support line — many offer free or low-cost options. You deserve support that’s personal, thoughtful, and real.

U.S. - Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Worldwide - Visit findahelpline.com for free, confidential resources

Your mental health matters and you don’t have to navigate tough moments alone.

To manage anxiety about artificial intelligence, there are proactive steps you can take.

Educate yourself about AI to understand its capabilities and limitations better: Learning about AI can make it feel less intimidating.

Engage in conversations about AI: Talking with others about your concerns can offer new perspectives and reduce feelings of isolation.

Practice mindfulness and stress-reduction techniques: Managing your anxiety effectively can help you focus on the present and reduce worries about the future.

Stay informed about AI developments: Understand how it's being integrated into society to help you feel more prepared and less anxious.

Understanding these fears and addressing them through education and dialogue can help alleviate the anxiety associated with AI.

You don’t have to be, though some concern is understandable. AI is changing fast, and it raises real questions, from job loss and scams to whether people can keep control of it. Some risks deserve attention. Others are far from certain, and no one knows exactly how AI will unfold. When we’re anxious, our minds jump to the worst outcome and can treat every headline as proof of a disastrous future.

It can help to follow reliable news sources and take breaks from stories that leave you on edge. When your thoughts race ahead, try a mindfulness practice to bring your attention back to today. If worry about AI is getting in the way of sleep or daily life, consider talking with a therapist or doctor.

The fear of AI doesn’t have a widely recognized specific term but is often considered a form of “technophobia,” which is the fear of advanced technology or complex devices. When this fear centers on AI, it can stem from concerns that the technology could surpass human intelligence and from the ethical consequences of machines making decisions that affect people’s lives. AI anxiety is rooted in the unknown future impact of AI on humanity.

On a societal level, increased reliance on AI could reduce human interaction and erode certain skills as machines take over more tasks. Understanding these potential negative effects can help develop strategies to mitigate them and ensure AI is used responsibly and ethically.

#9606. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

#9605. Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, said, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”

Homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who currently serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”

According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”

The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.

This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

#9603. 25 types of meditation and how to choose the right one

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

The benefits of meditation can reach across your well-being, from reducing stress and anxiety to improving focus and supporting mental and emotional health. But there’s a catch: meditation is a wide family of practices, and the type that works beautifully for your friend might leave you fidgety and frustrated.

We’ve grouped the many types of meditation into six families, so you can see how they relate before you pick one. Think of it as a menu. Try whichever one draws you in, and let your practice change as you do.

Meditation is a way to train our attention and awareness so we can be more present in the moment. Most types ask you to rest your focus somewhere, like the breath, a word, a sensation, or a movement, and to notice without judgment when your mind drifts, then return. That returning, over and over, is the practice.

What changes from one type to the next is where you place your attention and what you hope to cultivate. Some practices sharpen focus, while others cultivate compassion or help the body relax. Many share a thread of mindfulness, noticing where your attention drifts and gently coming back.

With a history rooted in the spiritual traditions of the East, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Taoism, meditation has long been recognized as a means to gain enlightenment, self-realization, and balance.

By exploring the different forms of meditation practice, you can discover what works best for you to enhance your overall well-being.

These practices share a common aim. You anchor your attention in the present moment and meet whatever arises without judgment. They're a good place to start if you're new to meditation.

Particularly accessible to beginners, mindfulness meditation invites you to immerse yourself in the present moment. It teaches you to observe your thoughts, feelings, and physical sensations without judgment. By focusing on the breath or the sensations in the body, rather than worries about the past or future, you learn to anchor yourself in the now. This can lead to reduced stress and improved well-being.

Read more: How to practice mindfulness meditation: 8 tips to get started

A body scan moves your attention slowly through the body, one area at a time, noticing sensation without trying to change it. It's a core mindfulness technique and a gentle way into the practice, since you always have your body to come back to. Many people use it to unwind before sleep.

Read more: Body scan meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice

Here the breath is your anchor. You rest your attention on each inhale and exhale, without trying to control the rhythm, and return to it whenever your mind wanders. Because your breath is always with you, this is one of the most portable practices you can carry into a stressful moment.

Read more: How to practice breath meditation to relieve stress

Mindful eating brings full attention to a meal through the senses: the color, smell, texture, and taste of your food, and the signals of hunger and fullness. It can support digestion and help you notice emotional eating patterns with more kindness.

Read more: How mindful eating can boost your mental and physical health

Focus is the whole point here. You rest your attention on one thing, a flame, a sound, or a word, and return to it each time the mind strays. Over time this can sharpen your attention and prepare you for deeper states.

Concentration meditation is a practice of focused attention, where the mind is directed toward a single point of reference, such as a candle flame, a sound, or the breath. This can help develop focus and attentiveness in everyday life and prepare the mind for deeper states of meditation. This practice can be especially helpful for students, professionals, or anyone looking to improve their cognitive abilities and productivity.

Read more: Concentration meditation: what is it and how to practice?

Mantra meditation involves the silent repetition of a word or phrase, known as a mantra, to focus the mind and bring deeper states of meditation. This practice can be found in many spiritual traditions worldwide and serves as a powerful tool for calming the mind, reducing stress, and enhancing spiritual growth and a sense of peace and clarity. If you find yourself easily distracted or struggling with a busy mind, mantra meditation can help you maintain focus.

Read more: Mantra meditation: what it is, benefits, and how to practice

Om meditation is a form of mantra practice built around chanting or silently repeating the sound "Om." The vibration of the sound gives the mind something to settle on, and many practitioners find the repetition grounding.

Read more: What is Om meditation? Plus, a step-by-step guide to practice

Also called trataka, candle meditation uses the soft glow of a flame as your focal point. You rest your gaze on the candle, placed at eye level a short distance away, and let it hold your attention. It's a visual anchor for anyone who finds eyes-closed practice restless.

Read more: Candle meditation: a step-by-step guide to practice at home

Visualization meditation guides you to picture a scene, place, or outcome in vivid detail, such as somewhere you feel calm and safe. By giving the mind a rich image to rest on, it can lower stress and support a sense of ease. Unlike open mindfulness, it actively directs the imagination.

Read more: Visualization meditation: 8 exercises to add to your practice

Warmth is the thread running through this family, directed toward yourself, the people you love, and even those you struggle with. These practices can enhance empathy and strengthen your relationships.

Compassion meditation aims to cultivate feelings of love, kindness, and compassion toward yourself and others. It involves silently directing sentiments of goodwill toward loved ones, acquaintances, and even people we might have a difficult relationship with. It encourages us to see beyond our differences, nurturing a sense of connectedness. A traditional example is Tonglen, a Tibetan practice that pairs the breath with compassion for suffering.

Read more: Compassion meditation: what it is, benefits, & how to practice

Loving-kindness, or Metta meditation, is a practice of cultivating an attitude of unconditional love and kindness towards all beings. It starts with developing a loving acceptance of yourself and gradually extends outward to include friends, family, strangers, and even those with whom we may have conflicts. This practice can help break down barriers of anger and division, promoting peace and connection. Though loving-kindness meditation and compassion meditation are closely related and often practiced together, loving-kindness meditation involves sending wishes of happiness, well-being, and peace to yourself and others, whereas compassion meditation specifically focuses on suffering, understanding it, feeling it, and wishing for it to be alleviated.

Read more: Loving-kindness meditation: what it is, how to practice and why

Gratitude meditation guides your attention toward what you appreciate, often by calling to mind a few people or moments you're thankful for. Practiced in the morning or evening, it can lower anxiety and support better sleep, and it pairs naturally with compassion practice.

Read more: How gratitude meditation can help reduce anxiety

Sitting still doesn't suit everyone. If stillness makes you restless, these practices let you meditate while the body is in motion, with your attention on each movement.

Moving meditation brings together deliberate movement and a focused mind. You move with purpose, noticing each step, stretch, or breath as you go. Yoga, tai chi, mindful stretching, and mindful dancing all fall under this heading, and it can be done almost anywhere.

Read more: The benefits of moving meditation and how to start practicing

Walking meditation means walking slowly and deliberately, with your attention fully on the act of walking: each step, the movement of your legs, the ground beneath your feet, and your breath. It turns an everyday activity into a practice you can take outdoors.

Read more: Walking meditation: how to practice and its benefits

Mindful movement is the broad practice of bringing present-moment awareness to how your body moves, whether through stretching, yoga, or simple everyday motion. It's mindfulness carried into the body rather than held in stillness.

Read more: What is mindful movement? Plus 9 ways to get started

Qigong is a traditional Chinese practice that combines movement, breathwork, and meditation to support balance and focus. In its active form you meditate while flowing through slow, deliberate movements, which makes it a bridge between exercise and stillness.

Read more: What is qigong? Benefits, types, and how to practice

Yoga nidra, sometimes called yogic sleep, is a guided rest practice done lying down. A teacher or recording leads you through stages of body scan, breath, and visualization into a state between waking and sleep. No yoga experience is needed, and it's often used for deep rest at bedtime.

Read more: What is yoga nidra? Plus, why it may be your new BFF at bedtime

A few practices are rooted in a specific lineage and tend to go deeper, often taught within a tradition or by a teacher. Several come from Buddhism, while others, like Transcendental Meditation and kundalini, come from Hindu and Vedic traditions.

Buddhist meditation is the broad tradition behind many of the best-known techniques, including Zen and Vipassana below, along with loving-kindness. If you want a feel for the tradition as a whole before exploring the specific practices, start here.

Read more: Buddhist meditation: types, techniques & how to practice

Zen meditation, or Zazen, is a disciplined form of meditation central to Zen Buddhism. You sit in a specific posture, focusing on the breath while observing thoughts and sensations as they arise and pass without attachment. Zazen emphasizes the importance of moment-to-moment awareness for a profound sense of peace and insight.

Read more: Zen meditation: how (and why) to start a Zen practice

Vipassana, which means "to see things as they really are," is one of India's most ancient techniques of meditation. It focuses on the deep interconnection between mind and body. Through disciplined attention to physical sensations, you can develop insight into the nature of impermanence, suffering, and egolessness, to move toward enlightenment and liberation. Vipassana meditation is challenging, yet rewarding, offering profound insights into our own minds.

Read more: Vipassana meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice

Transcendental Meditation comes from the Hindu and Vedic tradition and was brought to the West in the mid-20th century. It's a silent, mantra-based practice, typically done for about 20 minutes twice a day, and it's taught one-on-one by a certified teacher who gives you your mantra. It's described as effortless, letting the mantra gently carry the mind toward deep rest.

Read more: Transcendental Meditation versus mindfulness meditation

Kundalini meditation is a spiritual practice that aims to awaken what the tradition describes as an inner energy at the base of the spine, using breathwork, posture, and chanting. Practitioners describe effects in spiritual and energetic terms, which are rooted in belief rather than established science. Because the breathwork can be intense, check with your doctor first if you have respiratory, heart, or blood pressure concerns.

Read more: What is Kundalini meditation? Plus, how to try it yourself

Chakra meditation focuses attention on the body's energy centers, or chakras, often by visualizing each as a spinning wheel, chanting a sound for each one, or breathing into each area. As with kundalini, the idea of chakras comes from spiritual tradition and is described as belief rather than scientific fact.

Read more: Chakra meditation: what it is, benefits & how to practice

This family works from the body inward. The practices help your nervous system slow down and your muscles release tension, which makes them a good entry point when stress shows up physically.

Relaxation meditation is an umbrella term for any practice that helps the body release tension and the mind wind down. It often draws on breathing, body awareness, or guided sessions, and it's a gentle place to begin if deeper practices feel like a lot right now.

A sound bath, where you lie back and listen to instruments, is one example.

Read more: 5 relaxation meditations that actually work

Progressive muscle relaxation guides you to tense and then release each muscle group in turn, usually working from the feet up to the face. By targeting the physical side of stress, it can ease tension that anxiety stores in the body, and it pairs well with a body scan to finish.

Read more: What is progressive muscle relaxation (and how to practice it)

The six families above group the 25 types by where your attention goes. This table puts them side by side, so you can compare meditation types and see where to start.

There’s no one-size-fits-all approach to meditation, and your needs may change over time. The best meditation technique is the one that feels right for you now and fits into your life. These five steps can help you find it.

Reflect on your goals: Think about what you're hoping to achieve. Whether it's reducing stress, finding inner peace, or developing compassion, your goals can guide your choice of practice.

Experiment with different practices: Try out different meditation methods and resources, including the Calm app, online courses, and local meditation groups, for guided sessions in different styles.

Listen to your body and mind: Pay attention to how you feel during and after meditation. The right practice should leave you feeling calm and refreshed. If you feel frustrated or strained, try a different type.

Be patient and open-minded: Finding the meditation practice that works for you can take time. Approach each type with curiosity, allowing your experiences to guide your journey.

Seek guidance: If you're unsure where to start, seek advice from experienced practitioners or meditation teachers for support tailored to your personal journey.

Starting a meditation practice can bring greater mindfulness and improved emotional well-being. However, establishing a consistent practice can feel daunting. By bringing these tips into your approach, you can build a meditation practice that fits your life and becomes a source of strength and peace.

A consistent routine is important in establishing any new habit, including meditation. Identify a time of day when you can dedicate a few uninterrupted minutes to your practice. For many, morning meditation sets a positive tone for the day ahead. However, if evenings or another time fits your schedule better, make that your meditation moment. Find a quiet, comfortable spot where you can sit or lie down without distractions.

💙 Morning person? Try this Morning Meditation to set your tone for the rest of the day. Nighttime person? This Deep Rest meditation is for you.

Begin with just a few minutes each day. Even a short period of meditation can have significant benefits, and starting small makes the practice feel more manageable. As you become more comfortable with the process, you can gradually extend your meditation time.

💙 Begin your meditation journey with Jeff Warren in this Meditation for Beginners series.

Meditation is a personal experience, and there’s no single "right" way to do it. Many people form expectations based on others' descriptions, but each person's meditation journey is unique. You don’t need to empty your mind or feel bliss in every session. Notice your thoughts and feelings without judgment, and meet whatever comes up with kindness and curiosity.

💙 Explore how having Expectations can affect us and our lives with Tamara Levitt on the Daily Calm.

Physical discomfort can be a distraction during meditation. To help settle your body and prepare for stillness, consider some gentle stretching or mindful movement, such as yoga or tai chi, before you begin. This can help release tension in the body and allow you to sit more comfortably.

💙 Follow along with The Daily Move’s Releasing Stress session to help you unwind before settling down.

Guided meditations, available through apps, websites, or local classes, can provide verbal instructions and cues to lead you through the meditation process. They can introduce you to different types of meditation, help keep your focus, and offer insights into how to handle common challenges like wandering thoughts or restlessness.

💙 Try this guided meditation to help you with Reframing Difficult Thoughts whenever your thoughts start to overwhelm you.

It’s normal to encounter challenges as you begin your meditation practice. You might miss a day or find your mind wandering constantly. When this happens, treat yourself with kindness and compassion. Each time you notice your mind has drifted and come back to the present moment, you’re practicing.

💙 Practice this Loving Kindness meditation to guide you in cultivating feelings of kindness toward yourself and others.

Join a meditation group or find a community of practitioners that can provide support and a sense of connection. Sharing experiences with others on a similar path can be incredibly encouraging.

There’s no single agreed list, but these three approaches are often used to sort the many types of meditation:

Concentration meditation: You rest your attention on a single point of reference, such as the breath, a mantra, a sound, or a candle flame. When your mind wanders, you return to it.

Mindfulness meditation: You widen your awareness to include thoughts, sensations, and your surroundings as they arise. It is often taught as part of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR).

Loving-kindness meditation (Metta): You build goodwill and warmth toward others, starting with yourself.

The idea of levels in meditation can vary depending on the tradition or practice. A way to think of meditation depth might include the different types and states.

Physical relaxation: The initial stage where the body relaxes deeply

Concentration: The mind begins to focus, reducing distractions.

Mindful awareness: A state of heightened awareness of the present moment

Deepening peace: Inner silence becomes more profound.

Insight: Understanding about yourself and reality may arise

Blissful states: Experiences of joy or profound contentment

Transcendence: A sense of unity or oneness with all, often considered the deepest level of meditation

The power of a meditation practice can vary from person to person, depending on individual needs, preferences, and goals. Some may find mindfulness meditation helpful for managing stress and enhancing self-awareness, while others prefer the structured approach of Transcendental Meditation or the heart-opening practices of loving-kindness meditation.

Ultimately, the most ‘powerful’ type is the one you’ll keep practicing. Try a few to see which fits.

#9602. French authorities investigate claim of fraud over Picasso plates and medallions on sale

Pablo Picasso with a silver plate, in 1957. The artist had commissioned François Hugo to produce repoussé metal pieces from his designs © 2026 Succession Picasso/DACS, London; © Photo: Edward Quinn, © edwardquinn.com

A criminal investigation amid a family crisis casts a dark shadow over the illustrious history of the French studio Ateliers Hugo, which produced jewellery and silverware created by major artists of the 20th century. According to a legal source, the court of Aix-en-Provence in the south of France has opened an investigation following a complaint by the Picasso family.

On 10 March, Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, representing the nine heirs of the Spanish artist, filed a complaint alleging “fraud, counterfeiting, forgery and concealment of these felonies”. The file does not name the alleged perpetrators, and their identity is not presently known. The following month the Picasso family published a formal warning in the Gazette Drouot, titled “Hugo silverware”. It urged “all art market professionals and buyers to exercise the utmost vigilance”, following the appearance of what it described as “a large number” of illegitimate silver plates and gold medallions, valued at millions of euros.

Paloma Ruiz-Picasso, the daughter of Pablo, has filed a legal complaint on behalf of nine family members of the artist about the allegedly unauthorised works © Studio Cabrelli

The title refers to Ateliers Hugo, a goldsmith based in Aix-en-Provence. It was founded in 1933 by François Hugo (1899-1981), the great-grandson of the famous French author Victor Hugo. In 1955 Pablo Picasso, who since 1947 had created a variety of ceramics in Vallauris on the French Riviera, commissioned François Hugo to produce plates and dishes from similar designs in fine metals, using the traditional technique of repoussé. Later, the workshop reduced them into medallions and earrings. With the help of his brother, the painter Jean Hugo, who introduced him to artistic circles, François made jewellery designed by Salvador Dalí, Max Ernst, André Derain, Jean Arp, Jean Dubuffet, Roberto Matta, Jean Lurçat and Dorothea Tanning. In 1975, his son Pierre Hugo (1947-2023) took over the company. Pierre was followed by his son Nicolas (born 1989).

Members of the Picasso family and their lawyer, Jean-Jacques Neuer, who filed the complaint, declined to comment to The Art Newspaper. But their complaint alleges that “it has been discovered that the moulds of Picasso’s works were reused for unauthorised productions of silver and gold pieces, followed by duplicates, some of them bearing three times the same number, and unnumbered specimens”.

According to a source close to the investigation, the Picasso Administration, which represents the family, says it has discovered at least 17 complete or almost complete suspicious collections, amounting to hundreds of pieces. The first red flag was raised by the Museum of Old and New Art (Mona), a private Australian museum in Tasmania. According to this source, in May 2023 the museum informed the Picasso Administration of its doubts over plates it had bought at Sotheby’s in London. An auction catalogue of 13 October 2021 describes a “complete set of 24 silver plates” bearing the signature of the artist, completed with an additional “unnumbered proof of Visage aux mains”. The pieces were “accompanied by a certificate of authenticity issued by Pierre Hugo”. The lot was sold for £1.4m. Sotheby’s declined to comment for this story.

According to the legal files, the seller was the British dealer Mark Maurice, from a now dissolved gallery named Masterpiece. The source close to the investigation says the dealer allegedly produced documents showing that he had commissioned a set of plates and a set of medallions from the Ateliers Hugo between 2017 and 2020. Mark Maurice indicated he was “unable to respond” to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries “due to strict non-disclosure agreements in place”.

In summer 2023 the ceramics museum in Vallauris, Musée Magnelli, exhibited another collection of 24 silver plates as well as gold medallions attributed to Picasso.

In 2023, the Musée Magnelli in Vallauris exhibited plates and medallions attributed to Picasso Travelworld

According to the legal files, the Picasso Administration protested, having found that they bore no number, mark or punch, as legally required. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges these facts, but tells The Art Newspaper that the works exhibited at Musée Magnelli were so-called “author’s copies, made for the exhibition, duly indicating in the catalogue that they were not for sale”. He adds that he “recovered them and had them melted after the show”. Representatives for the museum did not respond to a request for comment.

In June 2023, as reported in the legal files, the French branch of the auction house Bonhams made a request to the Picasso Administration for the right to reproduce silverware for a catalogue. The auction house was planning a sale of 95 lots from the Ateliers Hugo collection, including works by Ernst, Derain and Cocteau, valued between €400 and €50,000 each. The most valuable were 59 pieces, “made by” or “after” Picasso.

On 26 September 2023 Bonhams was informed by the Picasso Administration that these pieces were considered to be “unauthorised” editions. The auction house then decided to “delay the whole sale”, just two days before it was due to take place. Nicolas Hugo acknowledges he “did initiate, in the wake of good results obtained at Bonhams UK, this sale of pieces”, produced, he says, by his “father and grandfather”. But, he adds, “When we were informed by dealers of the presence of possible duplicates, I agreed to withdraw the sale and collaborated with the Picasso Administration to identify them.”

Bonhams declined to comment, but according to the source close to the investigation, the lots attributed to Picasso were sequestered when a British financial company, Suros Capital, tried to recover them as collateral for a €256,000 loan. A spokesperson for Suros confirmed the operation to The Art Newspaper, adding that “it was secured against not only the Picasso pieces, but a range of assets which are progressively realised, so the company expects to recover the loan in full”.

In November 2023, according to the source close to the investigation, a representative for Bonhams France informed the Picasso Administration that a Spanish collector contacted the auction house to sell 24 silver plates, estimated at £900,000. Again, the auction house refused on the basis of Picasso Administration’s doubts about the objects’ authenticity. In the legal files, the Picasso Administration claims the same collector had sold another set of 24 silver plates and one of 24 gold medallions in private sales through Bonhams in London in 2022. Neither the British auction house nor the Spanish collector made any comment.

Nicolas Hugo, who says he has not been interviewed by the investigators, claims he has no knowledge of the proceedings and “is unaware of the content of the complaint” issued by the Picasso Administration. But, he says: “The criminal investigation can only deal with facts related to the time of my father and grandfather, therefore falling under the statute of limitations and concerning persons now deceased.” He adds that “the rights to reproduce the items disappeared with them, so I have never minted any of Picasso’s creations”, and he does not have the legal status of a goldsmith. However, he says: “I have signed some certificates of authenticity, but only to confirm my father’s own signature.”

In interviews with The Art Newspaper, Nicolas Hugo describes himself as a “self-taught art dealer”. When he was around 20 years old, he started to work as an assistant in galleries in Paris, before moving to London. He is now an agent for several artists and a curator. In 2022, the French magazine Les Hardis described him as a “mix of British and Saint-Germain-des-Prés charm”. “My father became very ill in 2018,” he told the magazine. “I had an epiphany. I decided to take over the workshop. I immersed myself completely,” and started to train in manufacturing jewels.

“From 2019,” he tells The Art Newspaper, “I became involved in the history of his workshop and helped my father to showcase this heritage, for memorial and commercial reasons. I set up exhibitions in places like Barcelona or Vallauris and initiated this sale of the fonds d’atelier at Bonhams Paris. I have not taken over my father’s company and was not his partner.”

Nicolas Hugo says: “There have been some duplicates on the market, dating from my father’s period, but I have no idea who had made them in the workshop.” He says he has “no idea who put a collection on sale at Sotheby’s in 2021” and knows “nothing of the three sets proposed by this Spanish collector to Bonhams in 2022 and 2023”.

The criminal investigation is still at the preliminary phase. It comes at a time when the company is already in limbo. Pierre Hugo died in October 2023 and his five children have turned down his inheritance. Nicolas Hugo’s brothers and sisters declined to comment to The Art Newspaper due to the ongoing investigation.

However, sources close to the case say that Pierre Hugo’s heirs’ inheritance came with a €2.5m tax debt. According to these sources, three of the Hugo siblings said in police interviews they were “not at all” aware of the conduct of the workshop by their brother Nicolas, who had succeeded their ailing father in 2019. The sources said the three Hugo siblings were on alert after learning that Bonhams Paris declined to sell the collection from the Ateliers Hugo in September 2023. According to the same sources, when Pierre Hugo died a month later, the three siblings went to the workshop and took 21 moulds of plates that they decided to hand over to the Picasso Administration. Three moulds from the set were missing and they did not find those for the medallions.

According to these sources, the three Hugo siblings explained to the investigators that, “knowing that the rights of reproduction were extinct, they wanted to be sure this would be respected”. The siblings also asserted that they “did not want in any way to be implicated in these operations and made it clear to the Picasso Administration”, according to the sources.

Together with his wife Monique Mueller, the Swiss collector built one of the largest private holdings of Pre-Columbian, African and Oceanic objects in Europe

Japanese enjoy art more than French, says curator of Lille Métropole Museum of Modern Art

The third-generation Ateliers Hugo has been casting artists’ creations using ancient techniques from the same workshop in the south of France for nearly 70 years
